a: National coats of arms are the official heraldic symbols of sovereign states, used on flags, currency, passports, and government buildings—examples include the Canadian arms with its maple leaf and royal lion and unicorn, the South African arms with its Khoisan figures and motto !ke e: /xarra //ke, and the Mexican eagle devouring a serpent on a cactus. State and provincial arms follow similar heraldic rules at a subnational level, such as the arms of Australian states (each featuring a distinct badge), Canadian provinces (often incorporating indigenous symbols), and German Lander (using traditional charges like the Brandenburg eagle or Saxon diamond crown). Municipal arms are among the most diverse heraldic expressions, with thousands of cities worldwide bearing coats of arms that incorporate local history, industry, geography, and patron saints—many use canting arms (visual puns on the city name, such as the bear in Berlin or the three crowns in Kingston upon Hull). Corporate heraldry includes arms granted or adopted by universities (like Oxford and Cambridge's elaborate arms), professional guilds (the Worshipful Company of Goldsmiths' leopard's head), banks, insurance companies, and other corporations that use heraldic-style logos to convey tradition, stability, and authority.

a: Military heraldry encompasses regimental coats of arms, cap badges, and colors (flags) that embody unit history and esprit de corps—the British Army maintains a complex system where each regiment has its own heraldic identity, including battle honors emblazoned on its colors. Heraldic ranks in the military appear in the epaulettes, collar tabs, and sleeve insignia derived from traditional heraldic symbols (like the British officer's pips and crowns or the US officer's eagles and stars). Naval heraldry includes naval ensigns (flags flown by warships), ship's badges (each Royal Navy vessel has an officially granted heraldic badge, a tradition established in 1918), and admirals' rank flags. Ecclesiastical heraldry governs the coats of arms of clergy, with specific rules for each rank: the Pope's arms feature the papal tiara and crossed keys of Saint Peter; cardinals use a red galero with fifteen tassels; bishops use a green galero with six tassels; and abbots use a black galero with three tassels. Diocesan arms represent the diocese rather than the bishop personally, often incorporating the diocese's patron saint or local symbols, while abbey arms represent monastic communities.

a: Sports heraldry includes club crests and badges used by football (soccer) clubs like Manchester United's red devil on a shield, Real Madrid's crowned monogram, and Barcelona's cross-and-bars—while not always strictly heraldic, they draw heavily on heraldic conventions. The Olympic rings (five interlocking colored rings) and the Olympic flame are modern heraldic symbols governed by the International Olympic Committee, appearing on the Olympic flag as a white field with the rings symbolizing the five continents. Heraldry in popular culture has experienced a massive revival through fantasy literature and media: J.R.R. Tolkien's Middle-earth heraldic systems (the White Tree of Gondor, the seven stars of the Dunedain), George R.R. Martin's Game of Thrones (the Stark direwolf, Lannister lion, Targaryen dragon), and the Harry Potter house crests (Gryffindor lion, Slytherin serpent, Ravenclaw eagle, Hufflepuff badger) have introduced millions of fans to heraldic concepts. Video games and role-playing games frequently feature heraldic design for factions, guilds, kingdoms, and player-customizable coats of arms—games like World of Warcraft, The Elder Scrolls, the Dragon Age series, and the Crusader Kings historical strategy game use heraldry as a core visual identifier for noble houses and realms.

a: Heraldry remains integral to state ceremonies: at the British State Opening of Parliament, the royal coat of arms is displayed prominently, the Crown Jewels are carried by officers in heraldic tabards, and the Sovereign's procession includes the heraldic banners of the quartered arms. Coronations are the most heraldically elaborate ceremonies—the anointing, investiture, and crowning involve the presentation of heraldic regalia (the orb, scepter, and ring), and the King of Arms proclaims the new monarch's style and titles. Heraldic funerals, historically reserved for nobility, featured the deceased's coat of arms on the hearse, hatchments (diamond-shaped memorial panels) displayed at the church, and the ceremonial breaking of the knight's sword and shield. Coats of arms appear on currency and stamps worldwide as marks of sovereignty and identity—the British Royal Mail uses a simplified royal arms as its insignia, the US Great Seal appears on the one-dollar bill, and many countries feature their national arms on coinage. The heraldic art revival of the late 20th and early 21st centuries has brought increased interest in proper heraldic design, with artists and designers creating new arms for municipalities, corporations, and individuals that respect traditional rules while using modern artistic techniques.
